p: The lab found Travis Hensley's DNA and her father's under the right hand. Under the left was a man nobody can name, and he isn't her father or Teo.
At the hearing Teo told it all in court, and their father took the stand and said he'd lied for nineteen years so nobody would come looking for his boy.
Ana told Dani she was the lawyer who turned her away at seventeen. In 2010 she knew which issue mattered, and she put it ninth.
Meredith's closing said a son would say anything to bring his father home.
Judge Esquibel took it under advisement, and in the hall Shannon Hensley looked at Dani a long time and said nothing.
Luis Ruiz. At the county jail in Brighton, waiting on the judge.
Ana Brennan. Waiting on the ruling like everybody else.
Joel Harlan. Dani's supervisor at the public defender's office.
Consuelo Baca. The neighbor from across the lot.
Meredith Sloane. The chief deputy district attorney.
Shannon Hensley. Travis's younger sister. He called her four minutes after eleven that night.

Wednesday, September 15, the recording named the county jail in Brighton again, and she took the call on the basement step, with the board on the step below her. The judge hadn't ruled. Ana had said two weeks, maybe four, and then she'd said not to count, and Dani had counted anyway, on the calendar on the side of the fridge, under the pizza magnet that held up her father's picture.

He didn't ask about the ruling. He asked whether Teo had gotten home all right on Tuesday, and what Lupe had said about her party, and whether the Rockies were really going to finish that far back. The food in Brighton was worse than the food in Sterling, he said, which he wouldn't have believed. Somebody near his phone kept asking a deputy what time it was.

It was her move, and had been since Sunday. She didn't take his knight. She brought her bishop out behind her own knight instead, so the two of them stood together in the middle of the board, and gave him the square by letter and number. He was quiet while he found it. Huh, he said. Then he gave her his.

They went on like that on the Wednesdays, a move each, and neither of them said a word about the court. On the twenty ninth, just before the minute warning, he said, Fifteen days, and she knew he'd been counting too.

October on Federal. Somebody downstairs left a load of towels in a dryer so long it smells like the inside of a car. Dicta's asleep on the rug. Pencil. Tonight we finish where we started a year ago, with the conclusion, because almost every question on the test turns on finding it, and because the hardest place to find one is a long document that sounds sure of itself.

The rule hasn't changed. Before anything else, find what the argument decides. Not what it says on the way there, not what it gives the other side, not the fact it's proudest of. What it decides. Then ask what everything else is for.

Take a hardware store. "Sunday mornings bring in less than the clerk costs. Most of my Sunday customers come in Saturday anyway. I'm closing Sundays starting in November." Three sentences, and one of them is a decision. The other two are reasons. A choice that says Sunday sales are weak is quoting a premise back at you. It's true, and it's wrong.

Long documents hide the conclusion in plain sight. A court order spends most of its pages on the evidence and the law and saves the decision for the end, and then it often adds what it isn't deciding. Read those last lines twice. A ruling that tells you what it doesn't decide has shown you exactly where its conclusion stops, and the trap answer always takes one more step.

How the exam asks it. Stems ask which choice most accurately expresses the main conclusion, or, for a passage, its main point. Say the decision in your own words before you look. The right answer matches it and doesn't go further.

A principle question hands you a judgment and asks for the rule behind it. Two tests. The rule has to cover the case, so that the rule plus the facts gets you all the way to the judgment. And it shouldn't drag in a condition the case never mentions.

My neighbor trimmed the branches of my maple that hang over her fence, and she says she was right to, because they drip sap on her car. Try three rules. People may cut anything that crosses onto their land: that covers her, and it also lets her cut my phone line. People may trim branches over their land when the branches damage their things: covers her, adds nothing. People should ask before they trim a neighbor's tree: it doesn't get you to her being right at all.

Know which way the question runs. If it asks for the principle that most helps justify an argument, a broad rule can still win, because broad still covers. If it asks which judgment conforms to a principle, walk the case through every condition the rule names and refuse to add one of your own.

How the exam asks it. Stems ask which principle, if valid, most helps to justify the reasoning, or which judgment most closely conforms to the principle. For the first, check that the rule reaches the conclusion. For the second, check every condition.

Must be true means there's no way out. Read each choice and try to picture the facts all true and the choice false. If you can picture it, the choice is gone. Most strongly supported is gentler. It wants the choice the facts make likely, and it still punishes anything the facts never touched.

The lost and found at the pool only takes things found on the deck. This towel is in the lost and found. So it was found on the deck. That has to be true. Was it left by a swimmer? Probably. Has to be? No. Somebody could have walked in off the street and dropped it.

Absence is where people overreach. When a search comes back empty, what you know is that the search came back empty. The thing you wanted could be somewhere the search didn't look. And watch "some," "most" and "all" on every line. One "most" in the facts can't hold up an "all" in the answer.

How the exam asks it. Stems ask which must also be true if the statements are true, or which is most strongly supported by the information. Test the first by trying to break it. Test the second by asking whether the facts make it likely, not merely possible.

Method questions ask how an argument works, not what it says. Describe the move in words that would fit a hundred arguments: answers with a counterexample, grants a point and limits it, applies a standard to the facts, shows the other side's rule leads somewhere they won't go. Then look for the choice that says that.

A coach agrees that the six a.m. practice is hard on the younger players and says that's a reason to shorten it, not to cancel it. She's granted the premise and refused the conclusion. A choice that says she attacks the younger players' complaint has the subject right and the move wrong, and that's the usual trap: it describes what the argument talks about instead of what it does.
Parallel reasoning asks for the same move in a different subject. Strip both arguments to their bones before you compare them, and match the bones, not the topic.
How the exam asks it. Stems ask how the argument proceeds, or which argument is most similar in its reasoning. Name the move in general words first, then match it.

In Reading Comprehension a legal document is a passage like any other, and you ask it the usual questions. What's it about? What would its author agree with? What's this paragraph doing? The trick is to let the author be exactly as careful as the author is. If a judge says what he isn't deciding, he isn't deciding it, and an answer that says he would is wrong however much it sounds like him.

An application question gives you a new case and asks which result the passage's reasoning supports. Pull the reasoning out first, as a rule with conditions, and then run the new case through it. If the new case has a fact the passage's reasoning depended on not being there, the result changes, and the trap is the answer that matches the old case's surface.
You've done all of this for a year on my cards. It's the same work on the test. Read for the decision, then read for what holds it up, then stop where the author stops.

How the exam asks it. Stems ask which situation is most analogous to one in the passage, or which result the author's reasoning would most clearly support. Extract the rule first, then test each case against all of it.

Method questions deserve one slow pass, because they're the ones where knowing the answer and choosing it come apart. You can understand an argument perfectly and still pick a description that's one word wrong.

Here's one. The city council wants to ban backyard fire pits, saying their smoke harms the neighbors' lungs. A resident answers that the restaurants on Main Street burn wood in their ovens every night, putting far more smoke into the same air, and that the council voted last spring not to restrict them. So if smoke were really the reason, the council would restrict the ovens too. The stem asks how the resident responds to the council, which makes it a method of reasoning question: not what the resident concludes, but how the reply proceeds.

Say the move first, in general words. The resident points to a similar case the council treats differently and says the council's own reason would cover it too. That's arguing from a parallel case to show an inconsistency. Now the choices, the way they'd come. It accuses council members of acting for personal gain. No. Nobody's gain comes up. It denies that fire pit smoke harms anyone. No. The resident never disputes the harm. It offers a counterexample to a general claim. Close and wrong: the council never claimed it restricts every source of smoke, so there's nothing for a counterexample to break. It argues that the restaurants should stop burning wood. The resident never asks for that. And it points to a similar case the council treats differently, to show its stated reason would also cover that case. That's the move, and it names both halves: the comparison, and what the comparison is for.

Notice how close the counterexample miss was. It did point at another case. It just gave that case the wrong job. Only the right choice described the whole move, the comparison and what it was for. When two method choices both sound right, ask which one would still be true if you described the argument to somebody who'd never heard it. The one that needs no help from you is usually the answer.

How the exam asks it. Method stems ask how the argument proceeds or how one speaker responds to another. Describe the move in general words first, then test every word of each choice against what the speaker actually did.
One more run through the arrows, all of it at once, because they're on nearly every test and they never stop being easy to get backward.

If, when, every and all put what follows them in front. Only if, requires and needs put what follows them in back. Unless and without mean if not, and the if not goes in front. No A unless B means A, then B. The flip of any arrow is the back denied, then the front denied. Denying a rule means the front happens and the back doesn't.

A not that crosses an and turns it to or. A not that crosses an or turns it to and. Deny all and you get some not. Deny some and you get none. Deny most and you get half or fewer. Two mosts of the same group overlap. Two somes don't have to.

The two moves that only look like logic are turning the arrow around and denying the front. Most flaws that come from a rule are one of those two, with a different coat on. And the right answer on a must be true question never needs anything you didn't read.
Say those to yourself once a week for as long as you're near this test, and before any job where somebody hands you a rule and asks what it lets them do. It's a long list. It's also the whole list.

How the exam asks it. Conditional reasoning runs through must be true, must be false, sufficient assumption, flaw, parallel and principle questions. Write the arrow and its flip before you read the choices.

One must be true question, start to finish, as a last look at the strictest stem on the test. The facts: every bus that leaves the depot before six goes out on the river route. None of the river route buses carry bikes. Bus 40 left the depot at five thirty.

Chain it before you read anything. Before six, then river route. River route, then no bikes. So before six, then no bikes. Bus 40 left before six, so Bus 40 carries no bikes. That's your prediction, and you have it before the choices.

Now the choices, the way they'd come. Bus 40 carries no bikes. That's the prediction. Some river route buses leave after six. Could be, can't be shown; the rule only tells you about buses that leave early. Every bus without bikes is on the river route. That's the second arrow turned around. Bus 40 is the only bus that left before six. Nothing says how many left early. And Bus 40 would carry bikes if it left after six. That denies the front. A late Bus 40 is outside the rule, and the rule doesn't say what it would carry.

Look at the four that lost. One could be true, one turns an arrow, one counts what nobody counted, and one denies the front. That's the whole family of wrong answers on these questions, and they come back on nearly every test. Chain first, predict, then match. If a choice needs a fact you didn't read, it's out.

How the exam asks it. Must be true stems ask what must also be true if the statements are true. Chain the rules first, then test each choice. If two seem to follow, reread the stem and check every arrow's direction.
Thursday, September 30, at twenty to eleven, Ana called her at her desk. It's here. Fourteen pages. A dryer door banged somewhere under her. Come read it. I'm not telling you on the phone.

Joel waved her out before she'd finished asking. On the bus she held her bag on her knees and didn't take the prep book out, and on Federal she went up the stairs two at a time, which she hadn't done since she was in her twenties.

Ana had read it twice already. Dani could tell from the pencil, a small tick at the top of every page and nothing else. Ana slid it across the desk, and this time she didn't go to the window. She sat back with her hands folded on the desk and watched Dani read it standing up, all fourteen pages. Esquibel started with the jacket. Page one. He said what the case had always been about, which was who, and then he spent thirteen more pages on it, and on the last one he wrote the paragraph she read three times.

Order of the District Court, Adams County, September 30, 2027, last paragraph. Because the motion is granted on this ground, the Court doesn't reach the defendant's remaining claims. The judgment of conviction is vacated, and the case is set for a new trial. The Court makes no finding as to who struck Mr. Hensley. It finds only that the verdict can no longer rest on the inference that the man in the red jacket was the defendant. SO ORDERED. Martin Esquibel, District Court Judge.
One sentence, Ana said from her chair. What's it about?
A. It's about the jacket. Once there's a second man, it can't hold the verdict.
B. It's about who did it. Somebody else hit Travis Hensley, and the judge says so.
C. It's about Phil. He had the cap in 2008 and never once showed it to the jury.
D. It's about the left hand. A second man's DNA, and no jury ever heard of it.

It's about the jacket, she says. Once there's a second man, the jacket can't hold the verdict. Ana says that's it, and lets her breath go. Page one, she says. He put it on page one. She doesn't say anything else about page one. She taps the last paragraph with her eraser instead. The verdict rested on one inference, and the inference needed one man, and there were two.

That's the one. Pencil down. Main idea. The order's subject from its first page is identification: the State's case rested on the inference that the man in the red jacket was Luis, and evidence of a second man under the nails means that inference can no longer carry the verdict. The DNA and the new trial are both parts of that one point.

Ana took the March card out of her shirt pocket, the one with the four lines on it, gone soft as a dish rag from riding in there against her pencil since spring, and put it down next to the order and ran her thumb down it line by line, never heard, couldn't have known, about what happened, probably an acquittal, and then down page eleven, where Esquibel had gone through the same four in about the same order. Page eleven. In Ana's copy of the 2010 opinion, that page had one sentence for the jacket. Esquibel had filled his.

Meredith's going to read this tonight with her shoes off, she said. The first thing she'll look for is a name. He doesn't give her one. So what's the rule that lets a judge set aside a verdict and not say who did it?
A. A verdict that hung on one link goes when the link breaks. No name needed.
B. A judge shouldn't set aside a verdict unless he can say who really did it.
C. A verdict should fall whenever the State's case had a weak link anywhere in it.
D. When DNA and an eyewitness don't agree, the court should believe the DNA.
Ana writes it on the back of the March card, small. ONE LINK. NO NAME NEEDED. That's what she'll find, if she reads it honest, she says. And she reads everything honest. That's her problem.

Right. Now say why. Principle. The verdict rested on one inference: the man in red who fought Travis was the man at the curb. New evidence of a second man breaks it. The rule that justifies the order lets a verdict fall when what it depended on is gone, whether or not anyone else is named.

Ana walked her as far as the door, and on the way she opened the top drawer of her desk and set her copy of the order in it, on top of the 2010 opinion with the coffee ring, squared the two of them up with her fingers, and bumped the drawer shut with her hip.

That night she took her copy over to Teo's, where he was in the carport under the hood of Bianca's car with a drop light on the beam. He wiped his hands on a shop rag a good while and took the pages and didn't look at them. Don't make me read it, I'll read it wrong, he said. Just tell me. Does it say Pa didn't do it?
A. "It says you didn't kill that man, Teo. Page nine, the part about the eye."
B. "It says Pa gets a new trial, Teo. That's the decision. It doesn't say who."
C. "It says a jury would probably let him go if they ever heard about the DNA."
D. "It says Pa didn't do it, Teo. A judge wrote that down and signed his name."

He reads the last paragraph himself, under the drop light. Not who, he says. She says not who. Good, he says, and it surprises her. I don't want a judge saying who. Then he turns pages till he finds the one about the eye, and reads that twice, and folds it back, and holds the order like that.

Good. That's how you read it. Main conclusion. The order's conclusion is the ruling: the conviction is vacated and there will be a new trial. A jury probably acquitting is the reason for it, and the order says outright it decides nothing about who struck the blow.

Friday, October 1, Joel came down the hall at nine with the order printed off the newspaper's story, stapled, with a paper clip on page eleven. He stood at the end of her desk. He couldn't close a door. He wasn't in his office.
Applications opened last month, he said. I put a new date on my letter. It didn't need anything else.
Then, with his eyes on the paper clip: I wrote it before you'd made up your mind. I didn't change a word. I didn't have to.

He tapped page eleven. Esquibel says a jury that heard all this would probably acquit. For that to follow, what does he have to believe about the one in 2008? He'd tried cases for twenty six years. He asked it as if he didn't know.
A. That the jury in 2008 believed the blood on the cuff came from the curb.
B. That nothing but the jacket put Pa at the curb. No witness. No confession.
C. That the jury in 2008 would've acquitted if it had heard about the cap.
D. That the jury in 2008 got it wrong and should've seen the hole on its own.

Nothing but the jacket ever put Pa at the curb, she tells him. No witness. No confession. That's the one I'd have gone after, he says, if I were her. And there's nothing there. He takes the paper clip off page eleven and puts it on her desk, for no reason, and goes back down the hall.

That's the one. Pencil down. Necessary assumption. The order concludes that the DNA would probably change the verdict, because it breaks the inference identifying Luis. That follows only if the conviction depended on that inference. Deny it, say a witness or a confession had put him at the curb, and a second profile under the nails wouldn't probably change anything.
Decision five. What he thinks of me.

Saturday, October 2, she drove up Highway 2 at noon with the order in a folder on the passenger seat. Consuelo had the front door open before she was out of the car. You're late. No, you're not late, I'm teasing you, get in here. I made caldo. Alma, move your papers. You want lemon? I raised her on this caldo, and look at her. Alma moved her spelling tests about four inches and kept hold of her red pen, and after that she looked up every time Dani moved.

When the bowls were in the sink Consuelo found her reading glasses and pushed the salt out of the way. Now. The whole thing, mija, slow. I want to hear every word he says about me. And don't you go skipping things to be nice to me. Alma does that and I hate it.

It took Dani forty minutes to read, with Consuelo stopping her twice. At the cap she put her hand flat on the oilcloth. That's right. That's what I told the lady on the telephone that night, the first thing, and she wrote it down, and then nobody ever read what she wrote. At the face she said, That's right too. I never saw it. I told them and I told them.
At the end she took off her glasses and folded them up and asked Dani what that judge thought of her, really, and not to be nice about it.
A. "He'd say the man you saw wasn't my father. That it was somebody else."
B. "He'd say you should've told that jury about the cap yourself, in 2008."
C. "He'd say you saw a man in red that night, and that's about all he'd say."
D. "He'd say you told it right in 2007, and they made it mean more than you said."

Consuelo doesn't say anything for a while. Then she says she went to confession every Saturday for a year after that trial, some weeks with the line out the door, for something she never did, and it took a judge in Brighton nineteen years to tell her so. She picks a piece of corn silk off the oilcloth and puts it in her apron pocket.

Right. Now say why. Would agree. The order recounts her description exactly, cap and all, and says she never saw a face. It says the State's identification rested on an inference built on her description. A judge who wrote that would agree she reported accurately and others read more into it.
Decision six. If they try it again.

Then she wanted to know what he'd put in there about Dani, and Dani found it for her on page two, where it said his daughter testified that she found the jacket in the washer the next morning, and it was wet, and the cycle was done. Consuelo wanted to know if that was what she'd said, and Dani said it was, word for word, at fifteen and again in September. Then he used yours right too, Consuelo said, and got up and put the rest of the caldo in a margarine tub for Dani to take home, and then a second tub, for the brother.
At half past three Consuelo went to change for the four o'clock Mass, and Alma walked Dani out to the car with her arms crossed against the wind. At the curb she stopped.

If they try him again, she's in it, isn't she. She'd have to sit up there and do it all again, at her age. She looked back at the porch, where the light was already on. Tell me what that paper means for her. What would she say different?
A. "She wouldn't have to. The order says a jury can't use what she saw anymore."
B. "Less, probably. They'd lean on the DNA now, and she'd be a small piece of it."
C. "She'd have to say it wasn't my father. That's what the order needs from her."
D. "Nothing different. She'd say what she saw, and this time they'd hear the cap."

Alma looks at the porch light for a while. Same as always, she says. She'd want to wear the brooch. Then she uncrosses her arms long enough to open Dani's car door for her, which is the nicest thing she's ever done for her, and goes back up the walk.

Good. That's how you read it. Application. The order says the first jury heard less than she told police: no cap. Applied to a new trial, her account stays the same and the jury hears all of it, alongside the DNA and the rest of the hearing evidence.
Decision seven. Under the left hand.

Wednesday, October 6, the recording named the county jail, and her father said Brennan had read him the whole order on the legal line the Friday after, every word, and he'd had her read the last part twice.
A new trial, he said. Brennan says don't get excited. I told her, Brennan, I'm sixty two. I don't get excited.
Then, quieter, with a TV going somewhere behind him: This other one. Under the left hand. Brennan says they don't know who he is. So what do they know, mija? About him?
She had the report by heart. Male. Not him. Not Teo. Run through the state and national databases. No match. It didn't say when.
Going only on the report, what must be true about the man under the left hand?
A. "He had hold of Travis that night, Pa. Sometime before the bar or after it."
B. "He's never been arrested, Pa. Not here, not anywhere. They'd have him."
C. "He's somebody who isn't you or Teo, Pa. No database they searched has him."
D. "He's the one at the curb, Pa. The one Consuelo saw run off in the cap."

That's all? She says that's all it has to be. He breathes out. Well, he says. I never saw him. I was looking at your brother the whole way out. Then he gives her his move, a rook along the back, and she gives him hers.

That's the one. Pencil down. Must be true. The report excludes Luis and Teo as the source of the second profile and says the state and national searches found no match. Those two things have to be true. Everything past them is a guess.
Decision eight. Not one word more.

Wednesday, October 13, after the call, she drove to Federal. Esquibel had set a hearing for Friday at half past one on a trial date and Ana's motion for bond, and Meredith hadn't said a word to anybody about either, which Ana said was either very good or the other thing.

Ana had a fresh card out, nothing on it. If she tries it, I stand up in front of twelve people and tell them about the man at the curb, she said. Not who. I never get who. Tell me what the record lets me say about him, and not one word more.
A. He was Unknown Male 1. That's the man Travis had hold of at the curb.
B. He was smaller than Travis and wore red. That's all anybody saw of him.
C. He was one of the refinery crew, in the same red work jacket that Pa wore.
D. He wore a cap. He ran on foot. Pa's truck had already left by then.

Ana writes it in capitals. CAP. ON FOOT. TRUCK GONE. Two of those are Consuelo's, she says. One's your brother's, and your father's. Twelve people can weigh that. She puts the card in her pocket behind the March one.

Right. Now say why. Most strongly supported. Consuelo saw a cap and a man running off on foot. Teo and Luis testified the truck had left the lot and was at a pump at 11:05. Each one is in the record, and none of them names anyone or says more than a witness said.
Friday, October 15, at four minutes to nine, Ana called her. Dani was at her desk with her coat still on. She filed. Motion to dismiss. One page.

Then Ana read her the paragraph that mattered, slowly, in her own flat voice, which made it sound like Ana had written it. The People bring a case to trial only when they believe they can prove it beyond a reasonable doubt, with evidence a jury may lawfully hear. Having reviewed the record of the September hearing, the People can't meet that burden as to who struck Mr. Hensley. The People don't ask the Court to find anything else. They move to dismiss.
That's all of it, Ana said. What's she standing on?
A. Drop a case when one of your main witnesses can't be relied on anymore.
B. Only try the cases you believe you can prove. Who did it isn't the test.
C. Drop a case when the victim's family tells you they're ready to let go.
D. Drop a case once a judge has said the man who was convicted is innocent.

Only try what you can prove, Dani says. Who did it isn't the test. She didn't say he didn't do it, Ana says. She said she can't prove he did. Those aren't the same, and she knows it better than anybody in that building. Watch her this afternoon. She'll say it out loud, and she won't say one word past it.

Good. That's how you read it. Principle. The motion says the People try a case only when they believe they can prove it beyond a reasonable doubt with admissible evidence, and that here they can't. It disclaims any other finding. The principle is about what the People can prove, not about whether he did it.

At half past one the courtroom was half empty. A deputy brought her father in through the side door, in what they gave you to wear at the county, and he sat down next to Ana without looking for anybody, and then looked anyway and found Dani behind the rail and nodded once. Teo had a bus up on a lift at the garage and couldn't get away. Shannon Hensley was in the second row on the State's side, by herself, with her purse on her knees.

Meredith stood up and left her notes on the table again. Judge, the People filed a motion to dismiss this morning, and I'd like to say on the record why, since Ms. Hensley is here and she's owed that much. If we try this case again, here's what a jury hears. They hear Mr. Ruiz say himself that he hit Mr. Hensley first in that bar and then lied to Detective Vigil about it for nineteen years. They hear Mrs. Baca say the man she saw had a ball cap on and ran off on foot. They hear a lab say there's a second man's DNA under the left hand and nobody knows whose. And they hear the son.

I've sat with that for two weeks, trying to work out what I'd stand up and answer it with, and I don't have anything. I'm not telling the Court he didn't do it. I'm telling the Court I can't prove that he did, and my office doesn't try cases it can't prove.

When she sat down Ana got up just long enough to say the defense had nothing to add, Judge, and sat back down, and Esquibel read the one page through again with his glasses down at the end of his nose and said he'd rule on it in writing. The deputy took her father back out the side door before anybody else had stood up. Ana turned around in her chair and leaned over the rail. So how'd she get there? she said. Don't tell me where she ended up, I heard where. Tell me how she walked it.
A. She walked a new trial through out loud and showed her proof couldn't carry it.
B. She argued Pa's innocent now, because the second profile clears him for good.
C. She gave up every fact our side proved at the hearing, and then she sat down.
D. She argued Esquibel got it wrong, and dropped it so she wouldn't have to appeal.

She called every witness she'd have to face, in order, in her own head, and then she asked herself what she'd answer it with, Ana says. And then she told him, which is nothing. Thirty years I've done this and I've seen that maybe twice. She says it like she'd buy Meredith a drink and never will.

That's the one. Pencil down. Method of reasoning. Meredith lays out what a jury at a retrial would hear, asks what she'd answer it with, and concludes that she can't meet her burden. She applies a standard to the evidence and draws the conclusion it forces.

Out in the hall it was hot by the elevators, the way it got in that building every afternoon once the sun came around to the tall windows, and Ana went off down the hall to find the clerk about some paperwork. Dani was at the drinking fountain with her bag on her shoulder when Shannon Hensley came out of the courtroom, crossed the hall, and stopped right in front of her, closer than she'd ever been, close enough that Dani could see she'd chewed all her lipstick off.

For a second she didn't say anything. She had the purse in both hands, the way she'd held it in the second row for three days of this, with her car keys already out and a little purple Rockies bat on the ring, the same purple as the pennants on the pole across from Consuelo's, older than the keys. Then she said it, not loud. Then who?
She wasn't crying. She sounded like somebody who'd had the answer every night since 2008 and was asking the question for the first time, and everybody else had already left the hall.
A. "I don't know. I'm sorry. I wish to God I could tell you, I really do."
B. "One of the men in red. Somebody from that bar. It had to be one of them."
C. "I don't know. Neither does the order. It says their reason failed."
D. "The man under his left hand. They'll find him now. I know they will."

Their reason, Shannon says. It was my reason too. I had a name. I said it every night. She doesn't ask anything else. She doesn't forgive anybody, and Dani doesn't ask her to. She goes down the stairs with one hand on the rail, the way she did in September.

Right. Now say why. Parallel reasoning. The order's shape: the reason given for concluding it was Luis fails, and nothing follows about who it was. Dani's answer has the same bones. She doesn't know who, the court doesn't either, and the old reason is gone.

Monday, October 18, there was a note on the mat under the mail slot when she came down for the bus. No stamp. Hardware store notepad, folded in thirds, the same square hand as January. We had our guy. That's the most dangerous sentence in police work, and I said it. G.V. He'd known the house. He still did.
She stood in the doorway in her coat and read it twice, and then she went back to the kitchen and put it on the fridge, under the magnet, next to her father's picture.

Wednesday, October 20, the last call from Brighton, she made her move and gave him the square, and he found it, and then he didn't give her one back. I'll do mine at the table, he said. Leave it how it is. Esquibel signed the dismissal the next day.

Friday, October 22, they let him out of the county jail in Brighton at twenty past ten, with a paper grocery bag folded over twice at the top. She'd parked as close as the signs let her. He stood on the sidewalk a while and looked up at nothing in particular, and she waited.
In the car he put the bag between his feet. You didn't promise me anything, he said. Every Wednesday I listened for it. She'd never said it once.
South on 85 she kept to the right lane. He watched the fields go by, and then the backs of warehouses, and then he started talking to the windshield.

Phil came out to the jail in May, before the trial, he said. He sat down and he said, Luis, they've got your girl on their list. He said if I had anything at all, anything that puts you somewhere else after you left that bar, a receipt, a tape, a guy behind a counter, then they don't need her. She never has to get up there.
Somewhere else. It was on the envelope in her own hand, under ENOUGH, since December. And Teo had told her in July about the receipt, balled up in the can by the pump.
And you had one. I had your brother on it. He said it to the windshield, the same as the rest.
A. "You're saying it's my fault, Pa. That I'm the reason they put you away."
B. "You threw that receipt out so nobody would ever find Teo on that tape."
C. "You could have kept me off that stand. You kept Teo off the receipt."
D. "Phil should've found you another way, Pa. That was his job, not yours."

He doesn't look at her. Yes, he says. Another mile of warehouses. He doesn't explain it yet, and he doesn't take any of it back. He'd waited all these years to say it in a car where she couldn't get up and leave.

Good. That's how you read it. Main conclusion. Everything he says builds to one claim: he had a way to keep his daughter off the stand, it would have put his son in the truck, and he chose to protect his son. Phil's offer and the receipt support it.
They were past the turn for 104th when he said the rest of it. I let them put you up there, he said. I knew what you'd say.
She kept her eyes on the road. A gravel truck ahead of them was dropping little stones off its tailgate, and she let it get farther off. For nineteen years I wasn't sure you didn't do it.
He nodded like she'd made a good move. Then we both know something now.
She took her right hand off the wheel and put it over his on the seat between them. It turned over under hers, the way it had at Sterling, and stayed.
They didn't say anything else till the house. He got out and stood on the walk looking at the porch, and she carried his bag in.

Saturday morning she went to Federal and asked Ana for box one. Ana didn't ask why. She brought it out of the closet and set it on the desk, and then she went downstairs to move a load from a washer to a dryer for the woman who ran the laundromat, which Dani had never seen her do. The notes were where they'd always been, loose in the front.

Phil Abrams's notes, loose in the front of box one. March 12, 2008. Galvan at prelim. Says client swung first. Get the bar tab. Who else was there? April 2, 2008. Client won't discuss the fight. Says nothing happened. May 14, 2008. Jail visit. Client says no stops. Ask again re daughter. May 20, 2008. Eyewitness expert? No funds. Ask again. June 3, 2008. Daughter tomorrow. Short cross. Be kind.

Ask again re daughter. Last December it had been lawyer shorthand she couldn't read. It read fine now. Ask him again about the stops, because of the daughter. Phil had told her father how to keep her off the stand and written down that he'd ask again. Whether he ever did, nothing in the box said. Three weeks later he'd written Daughter tomorrow. She put the page back in the pile and the lid back on the box. Ana came up the stairs a few minutes later smelling like dryer sheets and found her still sitting there with both hands flat on the lid, and didn't ask about that either, and went and filled the kettle.

Wednesday, October 27, twenty years to the day, she made supper for five at her mother's table: pork chops, rice, and green beans out of a can, which her father had eaten three nights running and said were as good as Ma's, which they weren't. He was sleeping on the pullout in the front room with the window cracked, because according to him the heat in that house could kill a horse, and every morning he was up at a quarter to five for a shift that didn't exist anymore, running the coffee maker in the dark.

The first morning she came up and he was at the fridge with his cup, in front of his own picture, him at forty one in the red jacket laughing at whoever had the camera, with Gene's note up next to it under the pizza magnet. Vigil wrote you this? he said. All those years a cop and he writes like a kid in the third grade. Leave it up. He's all right. She left it up, and so did he. Ma's lanyard was on the hook by the back door with the keys under it, and in five days he never put a hand on them, but he looked at them coming through for coffee, every single time.

Teo's truck came at six. Lupe had the door open before he'd got it in park, with Bianca hollering after her about cars. She was in her school coat and the paper crown from March, which Bianca said she'd slept in, and she had the knight off her fridge in both hands, tape and all. Bianca came up behind her with a pan of enchiladas under foil. She's been asking is it time since five o'clock this morning, Bianca said. Sorry. Hi. Her father had been standing in the kitchen doorway since half past five in a shirt Dani had bought him at the Walmart on 104th, and when the front door opened he didn't come any closer, and Lupe stopped on the mat and looked at him.
Are you a bad guy or a sad guy?

Lupe, Bianca said, from the walk. Teo was still out at the truck getting the Sprite out of the back. Dani had an answer ready, the kind grownups give kids about mistakes, and she didn't give it to her. She let him.

Some of both, mija, he said, and got down on one knee on the linoleum, slow, with a hand on the doorframe, because his knees weren't any good anymore. Okay. Your Tía would tell you anyway, so I'll tell you. I hit a man once, in a fight, in a bar, and I shouldn't have done it. You don't hit first. Then I told the police a lot of lies after, and your Tía, and everybody, for years. That's the bad part. And then I was up there in Sterling the whole time you were getting born and learning to walk and drawing horses with hats on them, and I didn't get to see one bit of it. Not one. That's the sad part.

Lupe asked which one was more, and he said to ask him next year, he'd know better by then. Lupe held up her knight. He'd done that in the library at Sterling with a pencil he had to give back, he said, and she walked right past him into the kitchen and climbed up on a chair to see what was in the pans, and behind her Teo came in last, and their father said his name, and Teo said Pa, and that was about as far as either of them got.
Teo washed up after supper and she dried, and every so often he flicked water at her, and she flicked it back, till Bianca said the two of them were worse than Lupe.

At seven, with the sink half done, nobody's phone rang. Her father noticed before anybody did. He looked up at the clock over the stove and then at the phone, face down on the counter, and went and sat down at the board at the end of the table, where it had been all week the way she'd left it on the twentieth, salt shaker for a rook and all. Lupe got up on the next chair on her knees with her chin on the table.

He picked up his knight, the one that had come out to face hers back in September. From the sink Dani saw where it was going before he let go, and there was no square left anywhere for her king. She had a plate in her hand. She put it in the cupboard. He set the knight down and didn't say which square, and Lupe looked from the knight on the board to the knight on her paper and up at him. It jumped. It's the only one that can, he said.

Later on, with the board still set up and Lupe asleep across two chairs under Teo's jacket, Dani sat down at the table with her laptop. The application had been open to the personal statement since Sunday, the first line written and the rest of the page empty, and she hadn't touched the first line since.
Personal statement, first line. The best witness I know is in her eighties, and she has never once said more than she saw.

Teo was at the sink drying his hands on one of Ma's old dish towels, and the prep book was by the laptop with the envelope in the back, her capitals on one side and her brother's name on the other. She shut the laptop. At the end of the table her father had started putting the pieces back where they began, his side and then hers, the salt shaker last. He looked past her at Teo, just once, and Teo stayed where he was with the towel, not coming over and not going for his coat either. Mija, her father said. King's pawn, two squares. New game. She pulled her chair in. Wednesday, seven o'clock, and no phone. Her move.
